data.prompt: Let f(x) = x^2. What is the average rate of change of f on the interval [1, 4]?
data.context: Use (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a) with a = 1 and b = 4. Watch the parentheses: f(4) means 4^2, not 4 times 2.
data.inputLabel: Average rate of change of f on [1, 4]
data.successMessage: Correct. f(4) = 16 and f(1) = 1, so the top is 15. The bottom is 4 - 1 = 3, and 15 / 3 = 5.
data.errorMessage: Not yet. Square each input on its own, subtract the outputs in the same order as the inputs, then divide.
data.explanation: f(4) - f(1) = 16 - 1 = 15 and 4 - 1 = 3, so the average rate of change is 15 / 3 = 5. Since f is increasing on [1, 4], the secant line slopes upward with slope 5.

data.footnote: A style guide settles disputed usage by declaring a house choice — it does not discover the one true answer.

items.label: A set of choices
items.text: A decision manual for questions where two reasonable answers exist. It picks one so everyone in a newsroom, publishing house, or school writes the same way.
items.example: Chicago says: omit the Oxford comma. AP says: leave it out.

items.label: Consistency
items.text: The main goal is not perfection — it is sameness. Readers should never notice the style flipping mid-article.

items.label: Changeable
items.text: Guides get revised every few years. When real-world usage shifts, the guide updates to match it.

rightColumn.heading: What a style guide is NOT

items.label: Not the grammar police
items.text: A style guide does not override hard grammar rules. No guide allows fragments or run-ons in formal writing.
items.example: "She went to the store. Because she was hungry." stays an error under every guide.

items.label: Not universal law
items.text: Two guides can give opposite answers to the same question, and both are correct within their own system. There is no Supreme Court of English.

items.label: Not eternal truth
items.text: A rule inside a guide can be dropped in the next edition. The guide follows usage; it does not command it.

steps.detail: Example: 'We lost the game our bench was tired.' Clue: two subject-verb pairs with nothing (or only a comma) between them.
steps.label: 1. Find the clauses
steps.text: Underline each subject-verb pair. If you find two or more independent clauses joined with no punctuation or only a comma, you have a run-on.

steps.detail: The relationship decides the punctuation: a sharp break, a close link, or a explained-by/but link.
steps.label: 2. Ask how the ideas relate
steps.text: Are they two separate statements, two closely related thoughts, or is one the cause, time, or contrast for the other?

steps.detail: 'We lost the game. Our bench was tired.'
steps.label: 3a. Sharp break → period
steps.text: Use a period (or question mark) to make two sentences when the ideas stand on their own.

steps.detail: 'We lost the game; our bench was tired.'
steps.label: 3b. Close link → semicolon
steps.text: Use a semicolon when the second clause follows closely from the first and no connecting word fits.

steps.label: 3c. Logical link → comma + FANBOYS or subordinating word
steps.text: Join with a comma plus and, but, or, nor, for, so, or yet, also — or use because, when, although, since, if, or that to make one clause depend on the other.

data.question: A car covers exactly 60 miles in exactly 1 hour, so its average speed is 60 mph. Which statement must be true?
data.context: The trip is 60 miles long and takes exactly 1 hour from start to finish.
choices: Its speed was 60 mph at every single instant during the hour
Its speed at the moment the hour ended was exactly 60 mph
Its speedometer may have read 80 mph at some instants and 40 mph at others
Its speed at the halfway point of the trip was exactly 60 mph
data.commonErrorLabel: Treating an average rate as an instantaneous rate

trapReasons.0: Dividing total distance by total time feels like it describes the whole drive, so it is easy to assume every moment matched it.
trapReasons.1: The end of the trip is a natural place to attach the average, but nothing about the clock's last instant is fixed by a trip-long average.
trapReasons.3: The midpoint of the distance feels special, yet an average over the whole hour says nothing about any particular moment.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: An average squeezes an entire hour into one number. That number is a ratio of totals, and many different speed histories produce the same totals. You could have cruised at a steady 60, or sped at 80 and crawled at 40, or stopped for coffee and then driven fast. All of them give 60 miles in 1 hour.
data.correctReasoning: Average speed is change in position divided by change in time: 60 miles divided by 1 hour is 60 mph. That fixes the distance and the time, not any single instant. Only if the speed never changed would the average and every instantaneous reading agree, and this trip is not stated to be constant. So the speedometer could indeed have shown 80 mph at some moments and 40 mph at others.
data.recoveryTip: Before using a rate, ask: does this number cover an interval or a single instant? If a stretch of time was involved, it is an average and any moment inside could have been faster or slower.

options.text: Dash — it shows a sharp break, and a dash is just a long hyphen.
